chief_complaint: severe epigastric pain radiating to back, high lipase
hpi_details: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe epigastric pain radiating to back, high lipase. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she has a severe case of acid reflux or a flare-up of indigestion from heavy, greasy meals.
concerns: She is worried that the pain shooting into her back means she is having a heart attack like her father had.
expectations: She hopes to receive fast-acting intravenous pain medication and a scan to figure out what is causing the agony.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Biliary (Gallstone) Pancreatitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management for Biliary (Gallstone) Pancreatitis emphasizes IV crystalloid resuscitation with analgesia, early oral feeding as tolerated rather than routine prolonged NPO status, and same-admission cholecystectomy once the pancreatitis resolves, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Biliary (Gallstone) Pancreatitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Perforated peptic ulcer without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Signs of shock or bruising around the umbilicus/flank (Cullen's/Grey Turner's sign) — suggests severe necrotizing pancreatitis.
management_principles: Plan for Biliary Pancreatitis: IV crystalloid resuscitation and analgesia, early oral feeding as tolerated (avoid routine prolonged NPO), same-admission cholecystectomy once resolved
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of severe epigastric pain radiating to back, with high lipase, consistent with a gallstone blocking the pancreatic duct.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Biliary Pancreatitis.
reference_soap.plan: Provide analgesia and goal-directed IV crystalloid resuscitation, and begin oral feeding as tolerated rather than routine prolonged NPO status. Evaluate for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction, which may require urgent ERCP. Arrange same-admission cholecystectomy after recovery from mild biliary pancreatitis.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Biliary Pancreatitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Biliary Pancreatitis

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone lodges at the ampulla of Vater and blocks the pancreatic duct, causing severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with markedly elevated lipase.
red_flags: Signs of shock or bruising around the umbilicus/flank (Cullen's/Grey Turner's sign) — suggests severe necrotizing pancreatitis

must_ask.say: Where is the pain, and does it go straight through to your back?
How severe is the pain, and is it constant?
Did this start after a heavy meal, and do you drink alcohol regularly?
Have you been told you have gallstones before?

history.answer: I have this terrible pain in my upper belly that shoots straight into my back, and it's been getting worse.
It started about two days ago and has been gradually building up rather than hitting me all at once.
It began right in the middle of my upper stomach, and it has stayed centered right there without shifting.
Yes, the pain pierces straight through to the middle of my back like a band.
It is a constant, severe, heavy ache that never completely lets up.
It is around an 8 out of 10 right now. It started at around a 4 and slowly escalated over the last two days.
Sitting up and leaning forward brings a tiny bit of relief, while lying flat on my back or trying to eat makes it much worse.
A few months back I had mild stomach cramps after heavy meals, but they always settled on their own within an hour.
At a routine checkup last year, an ultrasound showed I had small gallstones, but the doctor said they were harmless back then.
I have felt very nauseated and threw up twice yesterday, mostly clear fluid and stomach bile with no blood.
I passed gas this morning and had a normal bowel movement yesterday, with no diarrhea or blood in the toilet.
I haven't felt feverish or noticed any shaking chills.
My eyes look their normal color to me, and my urine hasn't turned dark brown nor has my stool turned pale.
history.topic: Jaundice and stool or urine changes

history.answer: No, I do not have any pain, burning, frequent urination, or blood when I pass urine.
I feel totally exhausted and drained, but I haven't felt dizzy or fainted.
No, I haven't had any abnormal spotting, bleeding, or unusual discharge.
No, my chest feels fine, and I haven't had any trouble breathing.
history.topic: Chest pain or shortness of breath

history.answer: The evening before this started, I ate fried chicken for dinner, but I didn't drink much alcohol at all.
history.topic: Recent fatty food and alcohol intake

history.answer: I took two acetaminophen tablets yesterday, but they did not touch the pain.
No, I have never had an irregular heartbeat, atrial fibrillation, or any vascular diseases.
I've been feeling completely wiped out and exhausted since this pain flared up.
I thought it was just a really bad case of acid reflux or severe indigestion from eating rich, greasy food.
I'm terrified that this terrible pain going into my back means I'm having a heart attack like my dad did.
I'm hoping you can give me strong pain medicine through an IV right away and do a scan to find out why it hurts so badly.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, liver trouble, or any other chronic medical issues.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any daily prescription medications, herbal remedies, or health supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications or food.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine at social dinners, maybe once or twice a month, and none this week.
I work full-time as an office administrator and live at home with my husband.
My mother had gallstones and had her gallbladder removed in her sixties, but there is no family history of pancreatic or gastrointestinal disease.
My menstrual cycles have been getting irregular over the past year, and my last period was about two months ago.
My husband had a vasectomy years ago, so there is no possibility that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Appears moderately distressed from abdominal discomfort, sitting slightly bent forward on the examination table.
Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 37.3°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Sclerae are anicteric and conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Mild epigastric distension noted without visible surgical scars, abdominal wall veins, or periumbilical bruising.
Hypoactive bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants; no abdominal bruits.
Marked tenderness on deep palpation over the epigastrium; abdomen remains soft without true muscular rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited in the epigastrium or other quadrants.
Negative Murphy's sign without inspiratory arrest during deep palpation of the right upper quadrant.
No tenderness at McBurney's point; psoas and obturator signs are negative.
Warm and dry skin with normal turgor; Cullen's sign and Grey Turner's sign are absent.
